Split conformal prediction reached its nominal coverage in all 24 settings I tested (within 0.006), but the sets were large when accuracy was low: at 90% coverage, temperature-scaled sets contained on average 63% (Qwen, English), 78% (Qwen, Arabic), 86% (Jais, English) and 89% (Jais, Arabic) of the options. The margin between the top two option probabilities separated correct from incorrect answers best for Qwen on English (AUROC 0.734) and worst for Jais on Arabic (0.579). Answering only the 20% most confident questions lowered Qwen's English error from 0.439 to 0.098. Jais showed a strong prior for option C (49% of English and 60% of Arabic predictions). Scoring Latin letters only cut the Arabic share to 29% but left accuracy, raw ECE and AUROC nearly unchanged. Because the two benchmarks differ in subject, level and number of options, I do not attribute differences between languages to language itself. Code is available at https://github.com/Mariyaaleem/arabic-english-medqa-uncertainty.
Machine Learning.comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 12 tables. Code: https://github.com/Mariyaaleem/arabic-english-medqa-uncertainty

Machine Learning.title: Reward Inflation: A Healthy Stimulus for Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Reward serves as the primary learning signal in reinforcement learning (RL). However, while reward magnitudes are typically held fixed throughout training, their temporal modulation remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose reward inflation, a gradual scaling of rewards over the course of training, and show that it can act as a healthy stimulus for RL. Theoretically, reward inflation induces an implicit recency weighting that upweights recent transitions during policy updates, enabling faster adaptation. We further show that reward inflation suppresses the emergence of dormant neurons by sustaining gradient signals as the policy saturates, suggesting a possible contribution to plasticity preservation. Empirical results on ALE games and MuJoCo tasks corroborate these findings, showing that an appropriate level of reward inflation benefits a broad range of tasks. Finally, we introduce Fed, an adaptive variant that adjusts the inflation level on the fly, and find that it often improves upon fixed inflation. Source code is available at https://github.com/northadventure/RewardInflation.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: Detection Is Not Early Warning: Evaluating Token-Level Alarms on Language Model Failures
Machine Learning.summary: Many failures of language models begin at a specific token, the onset. A monitor that reads the model during generation can classify the finished response, detect the failure once it is under way, or warn before it begins, and only a warning leaves time to stop or steer the generation. Monitors are usually evaluated with response-level metrics such as AUROC, which ignore when the monitor fires. We introduce PREWARN, an evaluation protocol for any failure with an annotated onset. It calibrates each monitor's threshold on validation data to an error rate chosen for the application, runs the monitor, and scores its alarms relative to the onset on all three tasks. As a case study we apply it to repetitive degeneration in three open language models, with early warning as the main task, using linear probes on activations and six untrained baselines. Response-level metrics saturate on this failure, and a rule that reads only the response length scores almost perfectly, while probes that AUROC ranks as equal warn very differently under PREWARN. Probes warn before the onset on most degenerate responses of two of the three models, low-rank adapters below the probe more than double the share of tokens just before the onset that it flags, largely by flagging degenerate responses long before the onset, and no untrained baseline warns much more often than random alarms. We release the probes with calibrated thresholds at https://huggingface.co/collections/marcodene/prewarn-degeneration-probes
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability as a Science. 30 pages (10 main text), 6 figures, 16 tables. Code: https://github.com/swiss-ai/degeneration-probe

Machine Learning.title: Systematic Evaluation of Training Data Generation Strategies for Machine Learning-Based Molecular and Materials Property Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Machine-learning (ML) models for molecular and materials property prediction are often trained on large datasets curated through arbitrary or generic sampling strategies. Such approaches can lead to the over- or under-representation of regions of chemical and materials space that are most relevant to the prediction task. An important challenge is therefore how to efficiently curate training data to maximize predictive performance while minimising the number of labelled examples required. Here, we systematically compare training data acquisition strategies for molecular and materials property prediction, ranging from random sampling to various active learning approaches. We evaluate their performance across different model classes, representations, datasets, and target properties. Our results show that the effectiveness of data acquisition strategies depend strongly on the interplay between the model, dataset, and prediction task, although uncertainty-based sampling generally outperforms alternative strategies. Based on these findings, we derive guidelines for selecting data acquisition strategies under a given labelling budget.

Machine Learning.title: ScrewSense: Mapping the Invisible - Anomaly Detection and Error Classification in Screwdriving Processes
Machine Learning.summary: The growing volume of process data generated by screwdriving systems, combined with advancements in computing power, data storage, and algorithms, is facilitating the application of artificial intelligence in this field. Accurately detecting and classifying screwdriving errors is crucial for ensuring product quality, avoiding costly rework in manufacturing, and supporting sustainability by facilitating the maintenance, reuse, and recycling of screw-connected products. In this context, machine learning approaches offer a promising alternative to traditional monitoring techniques, such as window-based methods or envelope curves. This study examines the use of deep learning techniques for anomaly detection and error classification in screwdriving processes. The data corpus consists of multivariate time series capturing process parameters, such as torque and rotation angle. For anomaly detection, the embedding space of a vector quantized variational autoencoder was analyzed. In terms of error classification, four different model architectures were evaluated. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of anomaly detection and confirm that deep learning models can distinguish between multiple error categories beyond traditional binary classification. This extends the capabilities of conventional monitoring approaches, achieving accuracies of up to 100%. Additionally, real-world data material was examined in order to further demonstrate model robustness. Overall the results indicate strong generalization capability and highlight the practical potential of the developed models for use in industrial screwdriving processes, eliminating the need for expert knowledge in error identification and significantly reducing manual effort and analysis time.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted manuscript, 59th CIRP Conference on Manufacturing Systems (CMS 2026). 6 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables

Machine Learning.title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
Machine Learning.summary: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every nonlinearity is a quadratic detection - an interference, a balanced reading or a camera - and the output is a Born probability: attention |<q|k>|^2, the form of the Born rule, normalised per row, a measured product for the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout; between detections, classical control rescales and re-encodes. With its denominators held at the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share to 10^-13. On e-SNLI natural language inference it reaches 77.45 +- 0.91 % accuracy, level with a same-size softmax transformer (76.62 +- 0.36 %) and an order-free bag of embeddings (77.79 %). Exactness buys the sum, not the best ranking. Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 44 % of pairs, of the 53 % some deletion changes, against 31-32 % for the softmax model's integrated gradients; the model's own gradient x input does as well (43 %), as does a bag of embeddings' (43 %, seed 0), and leave-one-out does better. Holding the denominators helps the low end: the five words ranked last change the answer in 1 %, against 6 % free. The same weights compile exactly to simulated optoelectronics, and their attention to qubits. On ibm_kingston, reading only the attention, the device gave the model's answers in all three Hadamard-test runs (the two shortest pairs and one without its deciding word) and both compute-uncompute runs (one circuit per overlap); uniform attention answers otherwise on two of the three inputs. With the device's row sums the evidence correlated with the exact one at 0.997 and 0.962 by Hadamard tests; with compute-uncompute, 0.971 and 0.48.
Machine Learning.comment: 40 pages, 9 figures, 14 tables. v4: compute-uncompute runs on ibm_kingston, a proposition on the shots the evidence needs, an order-free bag-of-embeddings baseline, and nulls for every device check. Code, trained models and every IBM job record: https://github.com/stein-research/reading-why (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23938333)

Machine Learning.title: FoMEMO: Towards Foundation Models for Expensive Multi-objective Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Expensive multi-objective optimization is a prevalent and crucial concern in many real-world scenarios, where sample-efficiency is vital due to the limited evaluations to recover the true Pareto front for decision making. Existing works either involve repeatedly fitting Gaussian process surrogates from scratch for each newly encountered problem, or rely on computationally demanding hypervolume-oriented policy learning for amortized optimization, making it challenging to achieve scalable pre-training and efficient yet robust adaptation for diverse emerging real-world applications. To address these challenges, we propose FoMEMO (Foundation Models for Expensive Multi-objective Optimization), which adopts a decomposition-based training paradigm that converts multi-objective optimization into preference-wise aggregated posterior learning tasks, enabling scalable pre-training on hundreds of millions of diverse synthetic datasets without relying on extensive real-world domain experiments. At test time, given observed trajectories from unseen problems and user preferences, the foundation model performs in-context posterior prediction and optimizes the derived acquisition functions for efficient candidate generation, achieving strong generalization and optimization performance without any subsequent model training or updates.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: costream: A Streaming Evaluation Protocol for Wearable Fall Detection
Machine Learning.summary: Wearable fall detectors are commonly evaluated on presegmented windows, where a fall window is extracted at an annotated impact and non-fall windows are sampled from fall-free signal. However, a deployed detector processes a continuous sensor stream in which the location of a fall is unknown. We specify a streaming evaluation protocol in which a detector traverses an unsegmented recording, aggregates window-level scores into a temporal confidence map, and emits timestamped events that are evaluated against the annotated fall. Holding the dataset, participant-wise splits, window construction and fitted models fixed, we compare presegmented and streaming evaluation on clinically verified real-world falls. The two protocols identify the same best-performing method overall, but select different methods in 6 of 20 model-window configurations, with the divergence associated with differences in the temporal clustering of false alarms. Streaming evaluation also exposes deployment-relevant quantities, including false alarm rate over elapsed monitoring time, detection delay, and the effect of the decision threshold, that are not captured by per-window evaluation. These results show that evaluation protocol can materially affect conclusions about wearable fall detectors and should be considered when assessing their suitability for continuous monitoring.

Machine Learning.title: A model of errors in transformers
Machine Learning.summary: We study the error rate of LLMs on tasks like arithmetic that require a deterministic output, and repetitive processing of tokens drawn from a small set of alternatives. We argue that incorrect predictions arise when small errors in the attention mechanism accumulate to cross a threshold, and use this insight to derive a quantitative two-parameter relationship between the accuracy and the complexity of the task. The two parameters vary with the prompt and the model; they can be interpreted in terms of an elementary noise rate, and the number of plausible erroneous tokens that can be predicted. Our analysis is inspired by an ``effective field theory'' perspective: the LLM's many raw parameters can be reorganized into just two parameters that govern the error rate. We perform extensive empirical tests, using Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro and DeepSeek R1, and find excellent agreement between the predicted and observed accuracy for a variety of tasks, although we also identify deviations in some cases. Our model provides an alternative to suggestions that errors made by LLMs on long repetitive tasks indicate the ``collapse of reasoning'', or an inability to express ``compositional'' functions. Finally, we show how to construct prompts to reduce the error rate.
Machine Learning.comment: (v1) 8+17pages (v2) Appendix A.4 expanded; consistent with published version

Machine Learning.title: Class-Competence Aggregation: Output-Layer Routing for Federated Multiclass DDoS Detection under Class-Concentrated Non-IID Data
Machine Learning.summary: Federated learning over distributed intrusion-detection sensors naturally produces \emph{class-concentrated} non-IID data, where an entire attack class is held by a single client and absent elsewhere. We show this collapses federated averaging in a specific, localized way: the output layer holds one decision boundary per class, and when a class's aggregation weight comes overwhelmingly from clients that have never seen it, its neuron receives an active anti-signal rather than mere dilution, collapsing to zero. On CIC-DDoS2019, standard FedAvg drives the concentrated LDAP class to $0.00 \pm 0.00\%$ F1 across every seed. We propose Class-Competence Aggregation (CCA), which aggregates the output layer per class using each client's own locally reported validation F1 as the weight, while hidden layers remain under standard size-weighted FedAvg. CCA requires no server-held auxiliary data and adds only one F1 scalar per class per round beyond the feature-scaling and class-count exchanges common to any federated pipeline. On our primary CNN-LSTM architecture, CCA alone raises LDAP F1 from $0\%$ to $84.83 \pm 1.65\%$, and the full method reaches $91.64 \pm 0.57\%$ macro F1, closing the federated-to-centralized gap from $-42.53$ to $-4.05$ points. Benchmarked against four other federated methods under identical partitions and seeds, CCA is the only one that recovers the concentrated class substantially and reliably; a $178\times$ smaller MLP shows the same qualitative recovery, though less completely, confirming the effect holds across architecture scale even as its magnitude varies. Results are validated across three seeds and replicated on a second dataset, CICIDS2017.
Machine Learning.comment: Under review in IEEE TIFS

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Binary Classification: Multiclass Machine Learning for Diabetes and Prediabetes Risk Prediction Using NHANES
Machine Learning.summary: Detecting diabetes risk early is important for preventing disease progression. Most existing machine learning approaches focus on binary classification, which limits their ability to capture intermediate risk states such as prediabetes. We develop a supervised learning framework to classify adults as normal, prediabetic, or diabetic using National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data. The framework uses routinely collected demographic, clinical, and lifestyle variables from 15,356 adults, with glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) used only to define labels and excluded from input features to prevent leakage. We compare conventional machine learning and transformer-based models and examine two binary formulations: normal versus prediabetes, and normal versus combined prediabetes and diabetes. Models are evaluated on a held-out test set using precision, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score. In the multiclass setting, performance is broadly consistent across models, with accuracy up to 0.72 and macro-averaged F1 of 0.70. Prediabetes remains the most challenging class, with F1 scores of 0.54 to 0.56 for conventional models and 0.53 to 0.55 for transformers, reflecting its overlap with both neighboring states. When the task is reduced to normal versus prediabetes, F1 scores rise modestly to 0.62 to 0.64. A more substantial improvement is observed under a broader screening formulation combining prediabetes and diabetes, with F1 scores of 0.73 to 0.74 across all models. These findings suggest that feature overlap along the biological continuum between normal and diabetic states contributes more to the difficulty of prediabetes detection than model architecture. Multiclass prediction provides a more clinically informative representation of metabolic risk progression but highlights a trade-off between clinically meaningful stratification and predictive accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: PatchKV: Weight-Space Compensation of KV Cache
Machine Learning.summary: Long-context inference with Large Language Models (LLMs) is bottlenecked by the linearly growing memory of the key-value (KV) cache. Existing compression methods reduce the cache through token eviction or approximation, but degrade sharply at aggressive compression budgets. We propose PatchKV, a training-free framework that compensates KV cache compression methods by carrying part of the context in the model's weights. PatchKV pairs an off-the-shelf compressed KV cache with a context-specific weight patch, which is computed once at context-loading time and served for downstream queries for the context. The weight patch is derived in closed form via ridge regression, by aligning the block-wise activations of context-derived reference query tokens under the full cache and the compressed cache. Once merged into the model, the patch leaves the forward graph and per-query inference cost unchanged in the single-context, multi-query setting. Across long-context QA (SCBench with up to 170K tokens, SQuAD, NIAH) and math (GSM8K) benchmarks on three model architectures, PatchKV consistently improves cache compression methods, suggesting an alternative direction to compensate them at aggressive budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/cusasak/PatchKV.
Machine Learning.comment: NeurIPS 2026. Code available at: https://github.com/cusasak/PatchKV

Machine Learning.title: Interpretable machine learning diagnosis of degradation mechanisms in lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells from temperature- and illumination-dependent electrical measurements
Machine Learning.summary: Machine learning coupled with device simulation is widely used to optimize thin-film solar cells, but almost exclusively in the forward direction, from device parameters to predicted performance. The inverse problem encountered after fabrication, namely identifying the mechanism that limits a given device, is still addressed by manual inspection of characterization data. In this work, both directions are examined for lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells using approximately 42,000 SCAPS-1D simulations. Replacing the Spiro-OMeTAD hole transport layer with CuI increases the simulated power conversion efficiency from 19.6\% to 21.6\%, almost entirely through the fill factor. Surrogate models trained and tested on a factorial parameter grid substantially overstate their predictive accuracy. An XGBoost regressor attains $R^2 = 0.9997$ on held-out grid points but only 0.58 on independently sampled devices, whereas training on a Latin hypercube design of comparable size restores $R^2 = 0.995$. For the inverse problem, a multi-label classifier identifies which of six degradation mechanisms are present from simulated temperature- and illumination-dependent open-circuit-voltage measurements. It achieves a macro $F_1$ score of 0.938, compared to 0.687 for a calibrated physics-rule baseline. The classifier does not, however, generalize to combinations of mechanisms absent from the training set.
Machine Learning.comment: Under review in RSC Advances

Machine Learning.title: Audit the Scaffold, Not the Checkpoint: A Stationarity Dichotomy for Recursive Self-Improvement in Agentic Coding
Machine Learning.summary: Rules for AI self-improvement often key on the model itself: has it been retrained, or are its weights frozen? We argue that, for AI coding agents, this check is incomplete, and we propose, but do not run, the experiment that would test it. An agent that keeps revising its own work runs into diminishing returns as long as the set of changes it can reach stays fixed, and can escape them only if that set grows. Our hypothesis is that the set can grow with the model untouched, because the software around the model, its scaffold of tools, tests and task breakdown, can be rewritten. If so, a frozen model guarantees a ceiling eventually but not steady behavior on the way there, and audits should track changes to the scaffold, not only to the model. The same criterion separates three things often lumped together: more search within a fixed setup, retraining the model during use (which can raise the ceiling), and rewriting the scaffold, which sits between them. Adding more agents does not lift the ceiling. Picking the best of several agents' answers reaches the best single agent's ceiling exactly, and only gets there faster. A majority vote could do better, but only if the agents fail on different tasks. In our tests, 30 agents from one model family failed together: some task defeated all of them, and a majority failed 23/55 (42%) of tasks. Our evidence is descriptive. On a public coding benchmark, the gain from each extra round of revision shrinks toward zero, though the unsolved tasks left to measure are also fewer and harder. Across 401 development sessions, the amount of code changed falls off from commit to commit, but programmers working before AI tools show the same pattern, so the data show that current practice levels off without showing why. We reach the criterion by treating repeated revision as a known machine-learning method, boosting, and note where real agents depart from it.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages main text, 47 pages total, 9 figures, 5 tables

Machine Learning.title: On the Difficulty of Sequence-Level Supervised Learning for Autoregressive Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: During the supervised learning phase, autoregressive language models are typically trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training data, which decomposes as a sum of token-level cross-entropies via teacher forcing. This objective is simple and efficient but potentially suffers from so-called exposure bias: a mismatch between the way the model is trained and the way it is used at inference time. Can we instead design sequence-level loss functions that incorporate inference-time decoding procedures, such as greedy decoding or autoregressive sampling? We show that two natural attempts lead to loss functions that are fundamentally flawed: unbounded below. We further show that these two flawed loss functions are intimately connected: using autoregressive Gumbel tricks, the sampling based loss is the expected greedy loss under Gumbel perturbations. Since the pathology stems from the dependence of the decoded sequence on the model parameters, we analyze the update direction obtained by applying a stop gradient on the sampling procedure, leading to a moment matching direction. While it is not the gradient of any loss function, we prove that it defines a valid descent direction in function space for the autoregressive negative log-likelihood. Despite these theoretical insights, the moment matching direction suffers from high variance. We conclude that teacher forcing may well be ``all you need'' for supervised learning of autoregressive models.

Machine Learning.title: Controlled Block Proximal Linearized Method for Nonconvex and Nonsmooth Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: In this paper, we consider multiblock nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization without assuming bounded iterates or coercivity of the original objective. We propose the Controlled Block Proximal Linearized (CBPL) method, whose control potentials establish boundedness while retaining the original objective, constraints and variables. We prove finite length and whole-sequence convergence to an effective critical point of the original objective, where one limiting subgradient annihilates all effective feasible directions. We establish finite total variation of the original objective and block functions, summable original effective residuals, and finite termination and linear or sublinear convergence rates for the original objective values. Scale orthogonality further gives full original criticality and, for homogeneous balancing controls, summable absolute objective errors with an $o(1/K)$ best-iterate bound. We establish a complete degeneracy theory for graph-regularized nonnegative factorizations: scale criticality is equivalent to graph collapse, and full criticality eliminates graph action; our controls prevent this collapse while retaining genuine reconstruction changes. Furthermore, our proposed method provides the practical, simple, and effective schemes for these applications, combining guaranteed convergence with explicit closed-form updates that can be applied directly to solve the original problems. We apply CBPL to graph-regularized sparse nonnegative matrix factorization with $\ell_0$-constraints ($\ell_0$-GSNMF), graph-regularized sparse nonnegative canonical polyadic (CP) decomposition with $\ell_0$-constraints ($\ell_0$-GSNCP), and graph-regularized sparse nonnegative independent-core matrix tri-factorization with $\ell_0$-constraints ($\ell_0$-GSNMTF). Numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness, convergence and structural control.

Machine Learning.title: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming
Machine Learning.summary: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Project page: egox-dream.github.io.

Machine Learning.title: From Data to Wisdom: Rethinking AI Through an Epistemic Lens
Machine Learning.summary: This paper proposes the Data-to-Wisdom Epistemic Architecture for AI (EAAI), a conceptual framework treating Data, Information, Knowledge, Understanding and Wisdom as five distinct but recursively interacting epistemic functions: observation, contextual interpretation, modeling and prediction, critical evaluation and informed judgment. Two observations motivate it: sequential readings of the Knowledge Pyramid obscure how these functions interact, and a targeted review of ten Bayesian reference books finds that prior distributions are defined mathematically while "prior information" and "prior knowledge" are not consistently distinguished as epistemic categories. A Bayesian interpretation relates the likelihood, prior and posterior distributions, posterior prediction, model checking and decision analysis to the five functions, without limiting EAAI to Bayesian systems. Extending "prior" in an epistemic sense, the paper distinguishes five kinds of prior context that can shape the model, the likelihood, the prior, evaluation and action. Three worked applications -- quantitative financial risk, actuarial modeling in health insurance and agentic AI for medical reimbursement claims -- show how EAAI structures the analysis of model assumptions, evidence interpretation, validation, dependencies and decision consequences, separating the prediction of a risk, the appraisal of its reliability and the justification of action. It draws implications for AI and machine learning, including evaluation by function, treating intermediate model outputs as evidence open to challenge and separating generation from appraisal, and compares EAAI with work on DIKW, Bayesian workflow, AI evaluation and risk governance. Its contributions are an epistemic vocabulary with recursive relationships, a more accessible reading of Bayesian methodology, a typology of prior context and clearer methodological terminology.
Machine Learning.comment: 23 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables

Machine Learning.title: Acoustic Respiratory Phase Detection on Mobile Devices
Machine Learning.summary: Breathing monitoring is important for well-being, stress regulation, and guided breathing exercises, yet existing approaches often rely on contact-based sensors or controlled environments. This paper presents a non-invasive framework for respiratory phase detection using acoustic signals recorded on commodity smartphones. The proposed hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture combines local spectral feature extraction with long-range temporal modeling to capture the cyclic structure of breathing. The model is evaluated using a Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) protocol on the Foundation Dataset and on an independent unseen test set comprising over 1300 breathing cycles and 2 hours of continuous recordings. The proposed 3-class formulation achieves 72.85% frame-level accuracy and 96.6% cycle-level exhalation detection efficiency in the LOSO evaluation, while achieving 76.94% frame-level accuracy, a Cohen's Kappa score of 0.65, and 99.2% cycle-level exhalation detection efficiency on the unseen test set. Results suggest that accurate respiratory monitoring may be achievable under data-constrained conditions, indicating that appropriate temporal modeling can learn transferable respiratory representations and generalize to previously unseen participants. An end-to-end ONNX deployment pipeline enables privacy-preserving on-device inference with latency below 20 ms, supporting real-time monitoring on mobile and wearable devices.

Machine Learning.title: HarmonICA: Quasi-Time-Invariant ICA for Motor Unit Decomposition during Dynamic Contractions
Machine Learning.summary: Decomposing surface electromyography (EMG) into the spike trains of individual motor neurons is a long-standing inverse problem and a key step toward motor-neuron-driven neural interfaces such as prosthetics and exoskeletons. The standard approach, independent component analysis (ICA) of the multichannel signal, assumes that the mixing from neurons to electrodes is stationary in time. This assumption fails during movement, when volume-conductor deformation makes the mixing time-varying, and current decomposition algorithms are correspondingly restricted to isometric contractions. We introduce HarmonICA, a quasi-time-invariant ICA formulation in which a static linear separator is preceded by a learned, low-rank, time-varying invertible transformation. The separator is trained with an independence loss on the uncompensated projection, and the transformation with a stationarity loss on the recovered source. Gradients are not shared between the two, so source extraction remains a classical linear-ICA problem while non-stationary distortion is absorbed by the transformation. The closed-form inverse of the transformation enables per-spike subtraction with a time-varying template during sequential peel-off. On a public simulated benchmark of dynamic high-density EMG with ground-truth spike trains, the method outperforms five adaptive ICA baselines at every recall threshold, recovering more units at a higher accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: Cloning is as Hard as Learning for Stabilizer States
Machine Learning.summary: The impossibility of simultaneously cloning non-orthogonal states lies at the foundations of quantum theory. Even when allowing for approximation errors, cloning an arbitrary unknown pure state requires as many initial copies as needed to fully learn the state. Rather than arbitrary unknown states, modern quantum learning theory often considers structured classes of states and exploits such structure to develop learning algorithms that outperform general-state tomography. This raises the question: How do the sample complexities of learning and cloning relate for such structured classes. We answer this question for an important class of states. Namely, for $n$-qubit stabilizer states, we show that the optimal sample complexity of cloning is $Θ(n)$. Thus, also for this structured class of states, cloning is as hard as learning. To prove this result, we relate stabilizer state cloning to a variant of the sample amplification problem for probability distributions that was recently introduced in classical learning theory. This allows us to obtain our cloning lower bounds in analogy to new sample amplification lower bounds for classes of distributions with an underlying linear structure. Our results provide a more fine-grained perspective on No-Cloning theorems, opening up connections from foundations to quantum learning theory and quantum cryptography.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 + 33 + 8 pages. Corrected small errors in classical sample amplification statements and proofs; new quantum cloning lower bound proof strategy that avoids an incorrect structured random purification claim in V1; new no-go theorems for structured random purification

Machine Learning.title: Edge-Gradient Augmentation under Reinforcement Learning for Temporal Graph
Machine Learning.summary: Temporal link prediction is critical for understand- ing dynamic interactions in evolving networks, informing appli- cations ranging from social network analysis to recommendation systems. Existing methods typically rely on raw temporal graph data, often neglecting explicit edge-change information that can significantly improve predictive performance. To address this gap, we propose edge-gradient reinforced learning (EG-RL), a framework that explicitly encodes edge-gradient events (edge births and deaths) through dedicated node and link encoding modules. EG-RL uses a policy-driven reinforcement-learning mechanism to dynamically select and augment the most infor- mative edge snapshots, guided by critic-based feedback to opti- mize prediction accuracy. The model comprises distinct modules for node encoding, link encoding, token mixing, and channel mixing, integrated through global pooling and followed by a two-layer multilayer perceptron classifier. Extensive experiments on multiple dynamic graph datasets demonstrate substantial gains in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and average precision. Ablation studies further confirm the necessity of adaptive edge-gradient augmentation and validate the effectiveness of the proposed encoding and reinforcement- learning mechanisms.

Machine Learning.title: Manifold Attracting Flow Matching: Physics-Constrained Sampling via Continuous Geometric Dynamics
Machine Learning.summary: Generating scientific data under previously unseen equality constraints requires satisfying the prescribed constraints without destroying the physical structure learned from data. Existing inference-time approaches often enforce physical constraints by repeatedly correcting predicted endpoints, but such discrete corrections can distort learned generative structure and introduce unstable feedback. In this work, we propose Manifold Attracting Flow Matching (MAFM), which continuously evolves a persistent anchor through an ODE whose dynamics drive it analytically toward the constraint manifold. Specifically, its geometric correction preserves model-guided tangent motion while prescribing the normal motion to contract constraint violations toward the manifold. This construction separates model tracking from constraint attraction and provides theoretical guarantees for residual contraction and local feedback stabilization. Experiments across geometric and partial differential equation benchmarks demonstrate improved generation quality over variant constraint-guided baselines while maintaining low constraint residuals. MAFM provides a flexible framework for coordinating learned physical structure and explicit constraints through controllable sampling dynamics, without retraining the underlying generative model.

Machine Learning.title: Sequential Membership Inference Attacks
Machine Learning.summary: Modern AI models are not static. They go through multiple updates in their lifecycles. We propose to design Sequential Membership Inference (SeMI) attacks leading to tighter privacy audits by exploiting the sequence of models and injecting a target canary at a controlled insertion time. First, for empirical mean computation, we develop SeMI*, an optimal SeMI attack to identify the presence of a target inserted at a specific insertion step. We derive the power of SeMI* to show that accessing the model sequence yields more powerful MI attacks than scrutinising only the final model. SeMI* exhibits an isolation property. Its power depends on the statistics obtained right before and after insertion of the target. Leveraging this insight, we develop practical white-box (accessing model gradients) and black-box (accessing loss) SeMI attacks against models trained with (DP-)SGD. Across datasets and models trained with (DP-)SGD, our experiments show that SeMI attacks achieve higher power than snapshot-independent baselines, and yield tighter privacy audits thanks to (a) control over the insertion time and (b) observations across the model sequence. Code is available at https://github.com/Thomick/pysemi.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Camera-ready version. Code at https://github.com/Thomick/pysemi

Machine Learning.title: RadRef: A Reference-Free Metric for Radiology Report Generation
Machine Learning.summary: AI-generated radiology reports are commonly evaluated against radiologist-authored references, limiting the applicability of standard reference-based metrics when no reference is available. We introduce RadRef, a reference-free metric that scores report claims against image-derived beliefs over a clinical finding vocabulary, weighted by relevance to the clinical indication. By evaluating findings beyond the report's stated claims, RadRef assesses omissions as well as unsupported assertions. On ReXVal, RadRef achieves $73.1\%$ agreement with radiologist rankings among non-tied same-radiograph report pairs, with $61.8\%$ pair coverage and $64.3\%$ tie-inclusive agreement. Its non-tied agreement is close to GREEN ($73.9\%$) and RadFact ($72.6\%$), with its strongest relative results on omissions. We further evaluate $100$ model-generated and $100$ radiologist-authored reports from $100$ MIMIC-CXR studies, independently annotated by two board-certified radiologists. On same-image omission rankings, RadRef attains Kendall's $τ_b = 0.295$, compared with $0.386$ between the readers. In separate paired comparisons across generated reports, no evaluated comparator significantly outperforms RadRef on omissions. The same image-grounded representation provides a false-finding readout, RadRef-FF, with $τ_b = 0.32$ on ReXVal and $0.29$ in the reader study. Controlled perturbations confirm that RadRef depends on the radiograph, report, and clinical indication. RadRef enables image-grounded evaluation before a radiologist-authored reference exists, supporting quality monitoring of report-generation systems in clinical settings, and complements reference-based metrics when one is available.

Machine Learning.title: One Byte, One Token: Byteifying a 27B Hybrid-Attention LLM with Self-Generated Data
Machine Learning.summary: Byte-level BPE fragments Chinese text (for Qwen3.8 on Chinese Wikipedia, 3.84 bytes per token on average; 64% of tokens are single characters) and hides spelling from the model. We ask whether an already-trained 27B subword model can be converted directly into a pure byte-level model (one byte, one token), without a patching structure or a local encoder, while keeping most of its ability. Starting from Qwen3.8-27B (48 Gated DeltaNet layers + 16 full-attention layers), we shrink the vocabulary from 248,320 to 384 entries (the 256 byte symbols already in the BPE vocabulary plus special ids), leave every other weight untouched, and continue training in a two-stage curriculum (encoding first, then reading) on 4.77 GB of supervised bytes: all dialogue/behavioral supervision is generated on-policy by the original model itself (character dictionary, word dictionary, general dialogue, coding sessions), and knowledge reading uses encyclopedia text (54% of supervised bytes). Training takes 178.6 h on 8xH200. On the same GPU and serving stack, the byte model's gap to the original falls within the paired bootstrap interval on MATH-500, HumanEval+, MMLU-Pro and non-thinking GSM8K, and it loses 4-6 points on C-Eval, thinking-mode GSM8K and non-thinking IFEval. Without thinking it leads on every character-level task (CUTE 75.2 -> 84.0, EXECUTE-zho 81.6 -> 93.9, our Chinese character suite 54.4 -> 64.0), but lookup knowledge about Chinese characters such as pronunciation and stroke count drops, and thinking does not recover it. The cost is throughput: per-step speed is identical, but each step yields 3-5x less output; Chinese characters per second is about 1/4 of the original, and prefill at 64K bytes is 6.5x slower. We also document four byte-model failure modes (greedy runaway, sampling breaking UTF-8, ineffective penalty terms on a small vocabulary, repetition) and their fixes.
Machine Learning.comment: v2: added two authors; text unchanged. Full text in English followed by the full text in Chinese. 39 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and task suite: https://huggingface.co/datasets/leiwhere/ld3-byte-eval

Machine Learning.title: Price co-movement and price information diverge across Nordic electricity zones after the energy crisis
Machine Learning.summary: After the 2021-2022 energy crisis, day-ahead prices in Nordic bidding zones no longer move together. We ask whether this divergence also changes the information carried by prices. The answer matters for integrating variable renewable energy (VRE), because it can help identify where wind and solar forecasts are worth producing, publishing, and using. We measured the co-movement of each Norwegian and Swedish zone with Germany-Luxembourg (DE-LU) in 2018-2025. We then used a single model, selected on 2024 data, to forecast 2025 prices at 11:00 on the previous day and tested which inputs improved accuracy in each zone. The zones moved alike until 2019, but co-movement diverged in Sweden in 2020 and in Norway in 2021, and the split has persisted. In 2024, four southern zones co-moved strongly with DE-LU (intraday correlations of 0.54-0.71), while four northern zones co-moved weakly (0.25-0.30). Yet price information did not follow this split. Previous-day neighbouring prices reduced mean absolute error by at most 2.2% in any zone, equally in coupled and isolated zones. Removing the transmission system operators' wind and solar forecasts increased mean absolute error by at most 6% in Norway, 8-16% in Sweden, and 31% in DE-LU, and the ordering held in 2024. Within Norway, the value of these forecasts showed no detectable dependence on reservoir filling. The divergence in co-movement was therefore not matched by a divergence in price information, which differed mainly between national generation systems. Thus, a zone's coupling to the continent does not indicate the value of VRE forecasts there.
Machine Learning.comment: Supplementary material in the ancillary file. Code and results: https://github.com/myptd/nordic-price-divergence

Machine Learning.title: Do Heavy Tails Help Diffusion? On the Subtle Trade-off Between Initialization and Training
Machine Learning.summary: Recent works have proposed incorporating heavy-tailed (HT) noise into diffusion- and flow-based generative models, with the goals of better recovering the tails of target distributions and improving generative diversity. This motivation is intuitive: if the data are heavy-tailed, HT noise may appear better matched than light-tailed (LT) Gaussian noise. However, replacing Gaussian noise by HT noise also changes the underlying estimation problem. In this paper, we revisit this paradigm through a combined theoretical and empirical study, establishing sampling-error bounds for two representative diffusion models driven by HT and LT noise. We show that HT diffusion models can achieve exponentially fast initialization, but accumulated training errors may offset this advantage. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support our theoretical findings. Our results call into question a growing design trend in generative modeling and challenge the use of HT noise to improve rare-region exploration.
Machine Learning.comment: 29 pages, 13 figures/tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: GNN-Enhanced TCN Algorithms for ECG Anomaly Detection
Machine Learning.summary: To a time series can be also given the structure of directed graph, opening the doors to the usage of graph neural networks (GNNs) in this context. In this paper we develop a new pipeline involving novel geometric deep learning models that merge the capabilities of ordinary TCNs with the ones of GNNs to solve an anomaly detection problem on electrocardiogram signals.
Machine Learning.comment: Follow-up to arXiv:2310.02774, which introduced a pipeline for an industrial dataset. A shortened version of that earlier paper appeared in the GSI 2025 proceedings. Here we extend the theoretical analysis and develop a pipeline tested on a benchmark dataset. Research conducted in 2025. Under journal peer review

Machine Learning.title: Uncertainty-Guided Label Rebalancing for CPS Safety Monitoring
Machine Learning.summary: Safety monitoring is essential for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) such as Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). However, unsafe events are rare in CPS operations, creating class imbalance that degrades data-driven safety predictors. Behavioral uncertainty, reflected in erratic control signals or rapid heading changes, is often correlated with safety outcomes: uncertain behaviors occur more often during unsafe operation. Yet safety monitoring rarely exploits it. We propose U-Balance, a supervised approach that leverages behavioral uncertainty to rebalance datasets before training a safety predictor. U-Balance first trains a GatedMLP-based uncertainty predictor that represents telemetry windows using distributional kinematic features and outputs an uncertainty score. Its uncertainty-guided label rebalancing (uLNR) mechanism probabilistically relabels $\textit{safe}$ windows with unusually high uncertainty as $\textit{unsafe}$, enriching the minority class without synthesizing data. A safety predictor is then trained on the rebalanced dataset. We evaluate U-Balance on a UAV benchmark and ForEnt, a quadruped-robot entrapment dataset. On UAV, U-Balance achieves F1/AUROC/AUPRC of $0.801/0.972/0.776$, outperforming the strongest safety-prediction baselines by 14.3/2.2/6.1 percentage points ($\textit{pp}$), respectively. While the strongest baseline varies across metrics (MLP for F1 and AUPRC; CNN for AUROC), U-Balance leads on all three. On ForEnt, it achieves $0.522/0.806/0.323$, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.4/9.2/1.4 $\textit{pp}$. Using the same Bi-LSTM safety predictor, uLNR outperforms the strongest alternative rebalancing methods by 17.0/4.1/8.2 $\textit{pp}$ on UAV and 2.3/6.5/1.9 on ForEnt. uLNR also outperforms Early and Late Fusion on both datasets. To our knowledge, this work is the first to use behavioral uncertainty for dataset rebalancing in CPS safety monitoring.
Machine Learning.comment: 14 pages (main content), 3 pages references, 6 figures, 6 tables

Machine Learning.title: Measurement-Calibrated Synthetic Pretraining for Rapid Adaptation of UAV Channel Predictors
Machine Learning.summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) links can change faster than route-specific channel data can be collected, so a channel predictor must often be adapted from only a short target-flight calibration segment. This paper studies measurement-calibrated synthetic pretraining as an offline source prior for rapid adaptation of channel state information (CSI) predictors. The synthetic source is calibrated to flight-only power evolution, temporal shape variation, frequency selectivity, and phase disturbance, and is then combined with measured source-flight fine-tuning before target-flight adaptation. Under chronological held-out flight splits, synthetic-to-real (S2R) fine-tuning reduces the measured-data budget needed to reach useful prediction in the low-data regime. For 50 ms-ahead prediction, it crosses a latest-channel-estimate persistence baseline with 50 measured training windows, roughly 0.5 s of 10 ms-spaced supervised windows, whereas training from scratch requires 600 windows. A target-prefix adaptation study further shows that a lightweight gated recurrent unit predictor can reuse the pretrained source prior with one prediction-layer update epoch, positioning measurement-calibrated synthetic pretraining as a reusable prior for scarce target-flight measurements.
Machine Learning.comment: 6 pages. Accepted version of a paper presented at the 2026 IEEE 104th Vehicular Technology Conference (VTC2026-Fall), Boston, MA, USA

Machine Learning.title: Rethinking Actions: Continuity-Aware Priors for World-Model Planning
Machine Learning.summary: Actions in expert demonstrations exhibit temporal structure. An ordered-versus-shuffled analysis across five environments confirms this dependence. We ask whether action proposals that better reflect expert continuity can improve visual world-model planning. Rather than imposing generic smoothness, we learn continuations from the temporal structure of demonstrated actions. Our locality-gated deep-kernel Gaussian-process prior, LG-DKGP, combines recent and longer-range executed action history, predicts a neural continuation, and learns a temporal Gaussian-process (GP) residual. A training-derived exploration scale initializes search around the corrected mean; a frozen world model evaluates progress toward the goal. Training first fits the neural mean, then jointly optimizes the prior with the GP residual using expert future actions. The resulting planner achieves 87.07\% macro success across five simulated tasks spanning native and fragment-level goal attainment, compared with 71.03\% for INTACT, 61.66\% for PRISM, and 58.66\% for LeWM. Component interventions and expert-relative action-structure comparisons support demonstration-informed continuations and reveal task-dependent effects of visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.

Machine Learning.title: Dataset Distillation via Drifting
Machine Learning.summary: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set of samples such that they directly approximate the per-class data distribution. Specifically, we "drift" our distilled data in the latent space of a feature extractor such that they move both toward the real data and away from each other without using a classification objective. We find that our drifted data cover the real distribution significantly better than existing methods while still serving as powerful training samples for classification. Furthermore, we showcase our method's use as a visualization tool for better interpreting models and extend it beyond images to other modalities. Our work advances the frontier of dataset distillation, offering a novel synthesis method and proposing distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation. More broadly, our findings help address the growing need to understand both data and models by uncovering more about how they interact.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project Page: https://drifting-distillation.github.io/

Machine Learning.title: Asymmetric Multimodal Learning with Decomposed JEPAs
Machine Learning.summary:
Cross-modal alignment is the standard objective for building multimodal representations. We show that alignment as a \emph{sole} objective is lossy wherever modalities are informationally asymmetric---where neither can express what the other carries. Visual question answering is an obvious case: a question is a selective relational operator probing a dense visual field whose fine-grained features no query recovers, so what alignment preserves is not what the task requires. We prove an \textbf{Alignment Redundancy Bound}: alignment-only Dirichlet energy minimization retains at most the redundant information atom $\Red(Z; X_1, X_2)$, annihilating private modality-specific structure $\Unq(Z; X_m)$ and cross-modal synergy $\Syn(Z; X_1, X_2)$.
  We introduce \textbf{Decomposed JEPA (D-JEPA)}, which factorizes latents into an aligned shared core and private modality-specific fibers. The shared core retains most of the structure alignment targets; the private fibers recover what alignment discards, via contextual masked prediction and asymmetric cross-subspace independence. Under information asymmetry, alignment-only training undergoes catastrophic semantic collapse on compositional reasoning benchmarks, surviving only on binary queries. D-JEPA averts this collapse, substantially improving downstream accuracy over both alignment-only and alignment-with-reconstruction baselines, and restoring a positive multimodal synergy gap in place of the baseline's inverted gap. Information-theoretic audits confirm that D-JEPA recovers most of the mutual information available from a frozen backbone, and causal fiber-swap interventions demonstrate that the recovered information is causally localized in the private fibers.
Machine Learning.comment: 15 pages, 12 tables, 3 figures

Machine Learning.title: Machine Learning for Scalable Multi-AP Coordination in IEEE 802.11bn Networks
Machine Learning.summary: As Wi-Fi deployments become denser, fully distributed random channel access no longer guarantees the required quality of service. The multi-access point coordination (MAPC) framework introduced in IEEE~802.11bn lets neighboring access points (APs) cooperate, but choosing which APs transmit together and how to configure them remains an open, computationally hard problem. We develop and validate a stack of machine learning (ML) coordination methods, progressing from lightweight hierarchical multi-armed bandits (H-MABs) to a generative pipeline built on graph neural networks (GNNs) and flow matching (FM). The methods are evaluated in simulation and on a hardware testbed, improving throughput over legacy access and scaling coordination to dozens of APs where analytical and search-based methods become intractable.

Machine Learning.title: DySR-GNN: Dynamic Sensor-Relationship Graph Neural Network for Root Cause Analysis in Automotive HiL Multivariate Time Series
Machine Learning.summary: Root-cause analysis in automotive Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) systems is challenging because faults can propagate across multiple interacting signals, making the most abnormal sensor different from the actual fault origin. This work proposes DySR-GNN, a Dynamic Sensor-Relationship Graph Neural Network for supervised multi-label root-cause identification in multivariate HiL time series. The approach jointly extracts temporal patterns within individual sensor signals and structural relationships across sensors. Each sensor is processed by a shared temporal encoder and combined with a trainable sensor-identity representation, from which a sparse relationship graph is reconstructed independently for every input window. This window-specific structure provides an explicit representation of the sensor relationships used for graph message passing and direct root-location prediction. Under a recording-disjoint evaluation protocol, the proposed model outperforms CNN--LSTM, Static GCN, Static GAT, and context-based variants, achieving a recording-level Macro-F1 of 0.9524, MCC of 0.9302, and strict exact-match accuracy of 0.8519. Analysis of the learned graphs reveals both persistent and state-dependent relationships among sensor variables. The results demonstrate that extracting adaptive relational structure alongside temporal representations can improve multi-label root-cause identification in complex automotive cyber--physical systems.

Machine Learning.title: A Dual-Branch Graph and Convolutional Network for Interpretable Movement EEG Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Decoding upper-limb movements from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is an important problem for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), but many deep learning models provide limited insight into the brain regions underlying their predictions. We propose a two-branch architecture that combines an LGGNet-inspired local-global graph branch with an EEGNet-style convolutional branch for movement-versus-rest classification. The graph branch groups 61 EEG electrodes into anatomically informed regions and learns their spatial relationships, providing a direct representation of the regions emphasized by the model. We evaluate the proposed architecture using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation on the Ofner upper-limb movement dataset. The model achieves a mean F1-score of 0.74 +/- 0.06 across subjects. Beyond classification performance, we analyze the learned graph structure to identify the regions with the strongest connectivity. Across all held-out subjects, the highest connectivity is consistently observed in the Parietal Left Low region, corresponding to electrodes P1 and P3. This region is opposite to the performed right-arm movements and lies within the posterior parietal area previously associated with upper-limb movement processing. These results show that incorporating a region-based graph into the decoder can provide an anatomically interpretable representation while maintaining effective movement classification, offering a practical approach toward more transparent EEG-based BCIs.

Machine Learning.title: Towards Democratising Low-Data Medical Image Classification: CPU-Trainable ZACH-ViT and Its Geometric Variants
Machine Learning.summary: Medical image classification in resource-constrained settings must contend with limited annotations and computational capacity. We evaluate four ZACH-ViT variants with linear, Euclidean prototype, Poincare and spherical heads alongside two compact multiple-instance-learning baselines. All models are trained from scratch with fewer than 260,000 parameters across seven MedMNIST+ datasets and three external benchmarks (PCam, ISIC2017 and Shenzhen tuberculosis radiographs). The low-data protocol uses 50 training images per class and five seeds, with validation-selected checkpoints at 23 and 47 epochs; a full-data reference uses one seed. Compact-TransMIL achieves the highest ten-dataset mean test Macro-F1 at 23 epochs (53.34%) and with full data (73.93%). At 47 epochs, ZACH-Linear narrowly leads (57.76% versus 57.54% for Compact-TransMIL). Extending training improves Macro-F1 in 239 of 300 paired comparisons. On ISIC2017, hZACH-Spherical has the highest 47-epoch low-data Macro-F1 (44.09% with SD 4.09%), whereas ZACH-EuclideanProto leads with full data (51.27%). We additionally conduct 40 CPU-only training runs on ISIC2017 and Shenzhen using four CPU threads; model-only single-image inference requires approximately 4-9 ms, while image decoding and preprocessing substantially increase end-to-end latency. The results demonstrate the feasibility of CPU-only training on the tested platform and the task- and regime-dependence of compact medical imaging under strict resource constraints.
Machine Learning.comment: 17 pages, 4 figures

Machine Learning.title: Fast approximation and learning of binary classification tasks in o-minimal structures using ReLU neural networks
Machine Learning.summary: We study binary classification tasks whose decision sets are given by definable sets in o-minimal expansions of the real field. Motivated by the cell decomposition theory of definable sets, we introduce traceable sets that isolate the analytical properties of definable sets used for fast approximation by ReLU neural networks. Under uniform bounds on the number of cells and a suitable extension assumption for the boundary functions, we prove that classifiers can be approximated in $L^p$ up to accuracy $\varepsilon>0$ by ReLU neural networks of size $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-p(n-1)/m})$, with depth independent of $\varepsilon$ and polynomially bounded weights. This establishes quantitative approximation rates for suitable definable collections in o-minimal structures using ReLU neural networks. Furthermore, the stated approximation rates are also derived for definable maps under similar geometric assumptions on their smoothness domains. We then obtain statistical learning rates for empirical risk minimization with hinge loss over the approximating ReLU neural network classes. For $N$ uniformly distributed samples, the predicted classifiers achieve expected misclassification error of order $N^{-m/(m+n-1)}$ up to an arbitrarily small polynomial loss.

Machine Learning.title: Learning pharmacokinetic dynamics with structured neural ODEs for precision dosing
Machine Learning.summary: Individualized dosing requires predicting how a patient's drug exposure would change under a different dose or schedule. However, a model that accurately predicts exposure at the current dose may not reliably predict what happens when treatment changes. We developed two neural models that learn pharmacokinetic dynamics from data without predefined pharmacokinetic equations. The first predicts exposure after a dose change, while the second also allows changes in dosing schedules. In simulations, the second model predicted exposure under new dosing schedules more accurately than competing neural models. On real data of kidney transplant recipients treated with tacrolimus, both models showed lower prediction errors than Bayesian estimation when predicting exposure at a later visit. These findings suggest that incorporating pharmacokinetic principles into neural models can improve predictions needed for individualized dosing.

Machine Learning.title: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs
Machine Learning.summary: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline. We release all 48 value-tuned model checkpoints at https://huggingface.co/sidicity/cultural-value-models
Machine Learning.comment: 38 pages, 31 figures, 26 tables

Machine Learning.title: Multimodal Zero-Shot Prediction for Transaction Data at Scale
Machine Learning.summary: Sequential financial transaction data are increasingly being used by financial institutions to train payment foundation models at scale, producing rich contextual embeddings that support applications such as fraud prevention, credit risk assessment, and offer personalization. However, such models are not designed for flexible instruction-following reasoning and require bespoke downstream models for each application. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) provide a natural-language interface for flexible transaction reasoning, yet naively serializing transaction histories into text representations is inefficient and costly. Multimodal fusion architectures bridge these paradigms, injecting transaction embeddings directly into flexible language reasoning pipelines. In this work, we present a systematic study of how transaction embeddings, pretrained at the scale of a global payments network, interact with LLM-based reasoning through embedding injection, transaction-language alignment, and instruction tuning. To do so, we train the Multimodal Instruction Network for Transactions (MINT), which combines a transaction encoder pretrained on billions of real-world payments with multimodal instruction tuning on millions of transaction question-answering examples. We evaluate predictive and extractive question answering, zero-shot generalization to unseen question types, and inference efficiency. Our results reveal a consistent trade-off: compact transaction embeddings improve predictive QA accuracy while substantially reducing input tokens, latency, and memory relative to a text-serialized baseline, whereas serialized histories remain highly competitive for extractive QA. Overall, our empirical findings provide a set of actionable insights and practical guidance for building multimodal transaction-aware language systems at network scale.
Machine Learning.comment: An abridged version of this paper was presented at the ICAIF'26 Workshop on Multimodal and Foundation Models in Banking

Machine Learning.title: A Free Knob: A Sensitivity Audit for Calibration in Threshold-based Evaluation
Machine Learning.summary: Many benchmarks for rare events score a prediction in three steps: pool the prediction and the target over spatial blocks, threshold each pooled field, and score the resulting contingency table. We show that at a fixed rare threshold the max-pooled Critical Success Index (CSI) cannot separate two different things: how well a system places events, and how well its amplitudes are calibrated. Sharp observations push many blocks above the threshold, while the attenuated predictions of squared-error regression leave those same blocks below it. A monotone calibration map is fitted on held-out data and applied separately to each system. The map needs no retraining and cannot change the order of any two pixels, so whatever part of a difference it reproduces cannot be evidence of better spatial ranking. We report how much of a reported difference the map removes. On SEVIR, two released checkpoints of one architecture differ by -29.5% in extreme-threshold CSI before the control and by +5.3% after it. Across 450 pairwise contrasts among 6 systems, how far apart two systems sit in pooled frequency bias predicts how far their CSI difference moves under the control (r = 0.896 when the map is fitted after pooling), and 64 contrasts reverse sign. At CasCast's published extreme-event operating point, calibration alone removes 88%-106% of the cascade's gain over its backbone across three controls. Calibration also reveals advantages hidden by a better-calibrated baseline. On geostationary infrared imagery, a larger share of the score can be explained by calibration as events get rarer. The problem therefore needs two things at the same time: a threshold that is fixed in advance, and a model whose output is poorly calibrated at that threshold. We recommend reporting pooled frequency bias and a symmetric held-out FreeKnob Audit alongside rare-event pool-and-threshold scores.
Machine Learning.comment: Code: https://github.com/munim110/free-knob

Machine Learning.title: HALight: Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Traffic Signal Control under Lane-Level Missing Observations
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning has shown great promise for traffic signal control. However, most existing methods rely on two key assumptions: (i) agents are assumed to be homogeneous with unified observation/action spaces; (ii) full and reliable lane-level traffic observations are available to all agents. In practice, urban road networks exhibit substantial structural heterogeneity (e.g., lane configurations and phase designs), while sensor failures and incomplete detector coverage often result in missing incoming lane measurements. Such issues can severely impair coordination and destabilize learning. To address these challenges, we propose HALight, a communication-enhanced heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for traffic signal control under lane-level missing observations. HALight supports intersection-specific observation and action modeling to accommodate heterogeneous intersections, and incorporates a lightweight one-hop neighborhood communication module to enrich spatial context when lane-level observations are partially unavailable. Moreover, HALight adopts a sequential policy update scheme to improve coordination among heterogeneous agents. Experimental results on two real-world road networks demonstrate that HALight outperforms representative homogeneous and heterogeneous baselines in terms of traffic efficiency and convergence behavior. The code and datasets used in this work are available at https://github.com/Huchenkaii/HALight.

Machine Learning.title: BELLS-O: Evaluating the Operational Trade-offs of LLM Supervision Systems
Machine Learning.summary: LLM supervision systems, namely input/output moderation filters and jailbreak detectors, are the primary safeguard against misuse in deployed AI applications, yet existing benchmarks are often vendor-biased, omit cost and latency, and rarely compare specialized guardrails against repurposed generalist LLMs. We present BELLS-O (Benchmark for the Evaluation of LLM Supervision Systems, Operational), an independent operational benchmark that evaluates 33 systems from 17 developers: specialized guardrails (e.g., Llama Guard 4, ShieldGemma-2B, Lakera Guard) and frontier generalists repurposed as supervisors (e.g., GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Grok 4.1 Fast), jointly on detection rate, false-positive rate, latency, and cost. We cover input/output moderation across 11 harm categories, jailbreak detection across 13 attack techniques, and prompt-injection detection, using in-house datasets built from handcrafted prompts, curated external samples, and quality-controlled synthetic generation, with synthetic moderation samples paraphrased to suppress generator fingerprints. Content-moderation runs are repeated five times and all rates reported with 95% intervals. The Pareto frontier reveals use-case-dependent tradeoffs. On content moderation, specialized supervisors are operationally ahead: top systems match the best generalist LLMs on detection (93-96%, no significant difference) at low false-positive rates while running ~5x faster; cost depends more on serving setup than on class. On jailbreak detection, generalist LLMs achieve higher median detection on three of four datasets and lower false-positive rates, but at higher latency and, for closed frontier models, 10-100x higher cost. On prompt injection, the two best dedicated detectors lead. We release the framework, an interactive leaderboard, and four datasets as a vendor-neutral basis for selecting safeguards under deployment constraints.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Track on Evaluations and Datasets). Previously presented at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Trustworthy AI for Good (AI4GOOD). 60 pages, 6 figures; 10-page main text plus appendices

Machine Learning.title: Semantic-Aware Task Clustering for Constructive and Cooperative Multi-Tasking
Machine Learning.summary: Cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) improves task execution performance by leveraging shared representations. However, as we demonstrated in [1], cooperative multi-tasking can be either constructive or destructive, depending on the semantic relationships among tasks. To ensure constructive cooperation, we propose a semantic-aware task clustering method for CMT-SemCom. We have formulated a sequential multi-stage optimization problem in which semantically aligned tasks are clustered once after a short initial training phase, and then end-to-end (E2E) joint training is conducted exclusively within the discovered groups. Specifically, the problem decomposes into two stages: (i) a semantic clustering problem leveraging hierarchical density-based spatial clustering, and (ii) an intra-cluster E2E CMT-SemCom learning problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, yielding accuracy gains compared to unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted in IEEE GLOBECOM 2026

Machine Learning.title: Look Here, Then Decide: Small Decision Models in a Harness Find Memory-Safety Vulnerabilities at Scale on Commodity GPUs
Machine Learning.summary:
We ask whether small, open-weight decision models can support vulnerability discovery in open-source software at scale and what the surrounding system must provide. These models answer a typed question in one forward pass, returning scores for the permitted answers rather than text. Our harness selects widely packaged C and C++ projects and uses deterministic incomplete-fix miners and shape localizers to decide where to look. Intern-Decision-4B, a 4B-parameter open-weight decision model, then scores every candidate function. The scores rank the queues rather than accept or reject candidates, apart from a low reach-score floor that some queues kept. The search uses no frontier model.
  Alone, the model is weak: it separates vulnerable from benign functions with AUC 0.73, but a vulnerable function from its own patch with only 0.56. It is more useful for ordering candidates. On 75 public CVEs from projects without any of our findings, the fixed function reached its repository's top 25 in 21% of cases, 1.4 times as often as under random order of the same queues. Recall is bounded mainly by where the localizers look. On the campaign's own queues the model's order placed 7.5 times more confirmed findings in the top 10 than random order, an observed, selection-biased upper bound. On three GB10 systems, the harness searched more than 4,000 projects at 900-1,100 repositories per hour. The campaign confirmed 187 memory-safety findings; by worst-case CVSS v3.1, 12 are critical, 148 high, 23 medium and 4 low. The decision step runs at 4.4 decisions per second on one GB10 and 9.8 on a consumer RTX 4090 gaming PC, with matching scores. A small decision model supports vulnerability discovery through prioritization, while deterministic analysis and verification remain essential. All confirmed findings are being disclosed to maintainers under coordinated disclosure before publication.
Machine Learning.comment: 24 pages, 2 figures

Machine Learning.title: When and How SignSGD Outperforms SGD: A Functional Scaling Law Perspective
Machine Learning.summary: We study how the sign operator interacts with gradient noise to shape the learning dynamics and scaling behavior of sign-based optimizers. In power-law kernel regression with diagonal features, we establish a functional scaling law (FSL) for SignSGD under general learning rate schedules. The FSL describes the learning dynamics through two processes: signal learning and noise forgetting. The key mechanism is noise-induced preconditioning: gradient noise smooths the sign operator, inducing an effective preconditioned SGD. Noise-curvature alignment enables this preconditioning to transform the effective Hessian from $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{H}^{1/2}$. The resulting dynamics exhibit faster signal learning but slower noise forgetting than SGD. This tradeoff yields a regime-dependent comparison with SGD: (i) SignSGD achieves improved data efficiency in the hard-task regime; (ii) both optimizers achieve the same data efficiency in the easy-task regime, but SignSGD maintains this efficiency at larger batch sizes, requiring fewer optimization steps for a fixed data budget. Power-law kernel regression experiments support the proposed mechanism and predicted scaling behavior. LLM pre-training experiments further suggest that the SignSGD FSL better captures the batch-size dependence of loss dynamics for sign-based optimizers than the original SGD FSL.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 as a spotlight paper

Machine Learning.title: Similarity-Guided Optimization Strategies for Approximate Network Symmetry Detection
Machine Learning.summary: Symmetry in complex networks is a structural property with broad implications for network function, dynamics, and robustness.
